section_summary: This section begins with a statistical analysis showing that, despite a fall in dollar value, the physical volume and relative importance of United States war-material exports to Japan remained high in 1938, especially petroleum, machinery, metals, and aircraft. Most of the section consists of congressional and public correspondence urging an embargo or other restrictions on supplies to Japan, together with State Department replies explaining its aeronautical-export policy and the absence of statutory authority to prohibit scrap-iron exports. A substantial group of memoranda concerns Chinese picketing and longshoremen’s refusal to load Japanese vessels at Oregon ports, the resulting diplomatic approaches, and the Department’s decision not to intervene. Other documents address the Nine-Power Treaty, proposed neutrality legislation, World Peace Foundation resolutions, and public appeals against aiding Japanese aggression in China.

subfiles.title: Statistical analysis of United States war-material exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Analyzes the value, volume, and composition of American exports useful for Japanese war-making during January-November 1938.
subfiles.summary: The statement reports that the value of war-material exports to Japan fell from about $157 million in 1937 to $142 million in 1938, but declined much less sharply than other American exports to Japan. It argues that lower commodity prices, rather than reduced physical volume, account for the decline. Petroleum, machinery, iron and steel, nonferrous metals, aircraft, and automobiles dominated the trade, while items legally classed as arms and ammunition formed only a small proportion.

subfiles.title: Tydings transmits Caleb Winslow’s letter
subfiles.about: Forwards a constituent’s protest about sales of war supplies to Japan and requests a reply suitable for transmission.
subfiles.summary: Senator Tydings encloses a letter from Caleb Winslow of Port Deposit, Maryland. He asks the Secretary of State to note it, return it, and provide a reply that Tydings can pass along to Winslow.

subfiles.title: Caleb Winslow protests supplies to Japan
subfiles.about: Asks whether the government is discouraging sales of scrap iron, munitions, and gasoline to the Japanese Army.
subfiles.summary: Winslow calls continued American supply of Japan foolish because it helps Japan shut China and Chinese trade behind a military barrier. He cites a statement based on a lecture by Walter Judd and expresses confidence that Senator Tydings shares his views.

subfiles.title: Hull replies to Tydings about Winslow’s protest
subfiles.about: Returns Winslow’s letter and supplies the Department’s statement on exports of war materials to Japan and China.
subfiles.summary: Hull acknowledges Tydings’s referral concerning scrap iron, munitions, and gasoline exports to Japan. He suggests that Tydings furnish Winslow with the enclosed Department of State statement and returns the original constituent letter.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to A. C. Barnshaw protest
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to another file for Barnshaw’s protest against scrap-iron shipments and Japanese bombing of Americans.
subfiles.summary: The note cross-references a December 25, 1938 letter from A. C. Barnshaw to file 393.115/3968. Its subject is protest against American scrap-iron shipments to Japan and the bombing of American civilians by Japanese forces.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to presidential inquiry on aircraft exports
subfiles.about: Points to a presidential memorandum asking whether aircraft-related exports to Japan could be reduced.
subfiles.summary: The file note directs researchers to a memorandum from the President dated December 10, 1938. The memorandum asked whether exports of aircraft, engines, parts, and accessories to Japan could be curtailed.

subfiles.title: Hinshaw forwards a constituent petition
subfiles.to: The President of the United States
subfiles.about: Forwards a petition from constituents opposing American support for Japan’s invasion of China.
subfiles.summary: Representative Hinshaw sends the President a petition signed by several constituents. The brief covering letter contains no policy argument of its own beyond transmitting their request.

subfiles.title: Petition against participation in Japanese aggression
subfiles.to: The President of the United States
subfiles.about: Urges every practicable measure to end American traffic in materials that supports Japan’s war in China.
subfiles.summary: The petition invokes the Nine-Power Treaty, the Kellogg Pact, civilian bombing, and the use of American planes, bombs, shells, scrap iron, oil, and trucks by Japan. It argues that American commerce makes the country a partner in the destruction of Chinese civilians. The signatories ask the President to use direct or indirect measures to end that traffic.

subfiles.title: Hull replies to Hinshaw’s petition
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the petition and sends copies of the Department’s statement on exports to China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hull states that the White House referred Hinshaw’s February 22 letter to the Department of State. He encloses twelve copies of the departmental statement for possible transmission to Hinshaw’s constituents.

subfiles.title: Church requests fifty copies of the Far Eastern statement
subfiles.about: Requests fifty copies of the Department’s statement for answering constituent communications about arms exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Church refers to Hull’s February 13 letter on arms and ammunition exports to Japan. He asks for fifty copies of the Department’s Far Eastern statement for use in constituent correspondence.

subfiles.title: Hull sends Church fifty statements
subfiles.about: Fulfills Church’s request for fifty copies of the Far Eastern statement.
subfiles.summary: Hull acknowledges Church’s March 1 request. The Department encloses fifty copies of its statement concerning the Far Eastern situation.

subfiles.title: Vermont Secretary of State acknowledges Department statement
subfiles.about: Thanks Moore for sending the Department’s statement on arms exports to China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Myrick acknowledges Moore’s February 16 letter and its enclosure. He expresses appreciation for the statement concerning arms, ammunition, and implements of war exported to China and Japan.

subfiles.title: Wilkins asks permission to circulate Moore’s letter
subfiles.about: Requests permission to share a State Department letter with the American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression and other interested persons.
subfiles.summary: Wilkins explains that he privately showed Moore’s November 28 letter on munitions and war materials to a friend. The friend wants to circulate it more broadly, but Wilkins seeks Moore’s consent before authorizing that use.

subfiles.title: Moore authorizes use of his November letter
subfiles.about: States that the Department has no objection to circulation of its November 28 letter.
subfiles.summary: Moore replies to Wilkins’s January 30 inquiry. He says there is no objection to Wilkins making whatever use he desires of the Department’s November letter.

subfiles.title: Walsh forwards Norton Kent’s inquiry
subfiles.about: Requests advice on how to answer a constituent asking about shipments of munitions to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Senator Walsh forwards Norton Kent’s letter to the Department. He asks that it be read and returned with suggestions for a suitable response.

subfiles.title: Kent asks Walsh about munitions shipments
subfiles.about: Asks whether anything is being done to stop American shipments of munitions to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Kent poses a direct question about government action against shipments to Japan. He asks Senator Walsh to explain what is being done.

subfiles.title: Hull answers Walsh’s referral
subfiles.about: Returns Kent’s letter and provides the Department’s statement for possible transmission.
subfiles.summary: Hull acknowledges Walsh’s March 5 letter enclosing Kent’s inquiry. He returns the constituent letter and encloses a statement on exports of munitions to China and Japan.

subfiles.title: Lodge forwards Norton Kent’s inquiry
subfiles.about: Seeks the Secretary’s comments on a duplicate inquiry from Norton Kent about munitions shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Lodge encloses Kent’s letter from the Boston University Department of Physics. He asks Hull for any comments the Department can provide.

subfiles.title: Kent asks Lodge about munitions shipments
subfiles.about: Asks whether the United States is acting to stop shipments of munitions to Japan.
subfiles.summary: This is substantially the same inquiry Kent sent to Senator Walsh. He asks Senator Lodge to report what, if anything, the government is doing.

subfiles.title: Welles replies to Lodge on export policy
subfiles.about: Explains the Department’s aeronautical-export policy and supplies supporting statements and reports for Kent.
subfiles.summary: Welles encloses the Department’s general statement, the National Munitions Control Board’s Third Annual Report, and the January 12 press release. He reports that the previously noncooperating company has agreed to comply, so all American manufacturers and exporters of aeronautical supplies are following the policy against supplying forces that bomb civilians. Kent’s letter is returned for Lodge’s reply.

subfiles.title: Jones thanks Moore for considering foundation resolutions
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Moore’s response to World Peace Foundation resolutions and receipt of the Department’s export statement.
subfiles.summary: Jones thanks Moore for saying that the trustees’ February 11 resolutions will receive departmental consideration. He also acknowledges the Department’s March 1 statement on war-material exports to China and Japan.

subfiles.title: Moore responds to World Peace Foundation resolutions
subfiles.about: Promises careful consideration of the foundation’s resolutions and encloses the Department’s export statement.
subfiles.summary: Moore thanks Jones for communicating the resolutions adopted by the trustees on February 11. He assures Jones that their views will receive careful consideration and sends the Department’s statement on exports to China and Japan.

subfiles.title: World Peace Foundation submits policy resolutions
subfiles.about: Transmits resolutions advocating an end to supplies for Japan, military preparedness, and broader presidential discretion under neutrality legislation.
subfiles.summary: The trustees declare continued American supply of Japan’s war in China intolerable and call for material sacrifice to end it. They also support adequate American preparedness and reaffirm a 1935 position favoring presidential discretion over embargoes and trade restrictions. Jones invites Hull to use the resolutions as he considers advisable.

subfiles.title: Charge slip for file 894.24 enclosures
subfiles.about: Records the temporary charging or circulation of enclosures from file 894.24.
subfiles.summary: The page is an administrative charge slip containing dates, numbers, and clerks’ notations. It contains no substantive policy discussion.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Japanese concern over neutrality legislation
subfiles.about: Points to a memorandum of conversation on Japanese business interest in prospective American neutrality legislation.
subfiles.summary: The note cross-references file 894.6363/326. It identifies a February 14 memorandum of conversation with A. D. De Friest concerning how new United States neutrality legislation might affect Japanese business interests.

subfiles.title: Hackworth advises on scrap iron and the Nine-Power Treaty
subfiles.about: Recommends telling Senator McNary that scrap-iron exports do not violate the Nine-Power Treaty and cannot be prohibited under existing legislation.
subfiles.summary: Hackworth advises a concise legal response to McNary. He concludes that a treaty violation could not be successfully maintained and that no law either prevents the shipments or authorizes their prevention.

subfiles.title: McNary forwards Logan’s argument on scrap iron
subfiles.about: Requests State Department views on an Oregon lawyer’s contention that scrap-iron shipments to Japan breach the Nine-Power Treaty.
subfiles.summary: McNary encloses John F. Logan’s letter and supporting data. He asks Hull to evaluate the legal claim that shipment of munitions or scrap iron to Japan violates the treaty.

subfiles.title: Logan argues that scrap-iron exports violate treaty obligations
subfiles.about: Argues that allowing scrap-iron exports to Japan violates the Nine-Power Treaty and undermines American aid to China.
subfiles.summary: Logan describes Northwest agitation and longshoremen’s refusal to load scrap iron at Astoria, Marshfield, and Portland. Working with Joe P. Price and Fred H. Lysons on behalf of Chinese groups, he contends that the treaty and Open Door policy require action against such shipments. He contrasts American credit to China with continued supply of Japan and reports broad local support for the longshoremen.

subfiles.title: Hull rejects the treaty argument against scrap-iron exports
subfiles.about: States that scrap-iron exports do not violate the Nine-Power Treaty and cannot be prohibited under current law.
subfiles.summary: Hull encloses a copy of the treaty and says its terms cannot sustain Logan’s argument. He adds that no existing legislation prohibits or authorizes prohibition of scrap-iron exports and returns McNary’s enclosures.

subfiles.title: Church requests fifty additional statements
subfiles.about: Asks for fifty more copies of the Department’s statement on the Far Eastern situation.
subfiles.summary: Church refers to the earlier correspondence filed under 894.24/612. He requests an additional batch of fifty statements for distribution.

subfiles.title: Welles sends Church additional statements and licensing totals
subfiles.about: Provides fifty statements and current figures for licensed arms exports to China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Welles sends the requested copies but explains that statistical blanks were left open because values change weekly. He supplies licensing totals for arms, ammunition, and implements of war to China and Japan from July 1, 1937 through March 18, 1939, and offers future updates.

subfiles.title: Welles asks Hamilton to draft a reply
subfiles.about: Directs Hamilton to draft an appropriate response to Mr. and Mrs. Baker.
subfiles.summary: Welles notes that he does not remember the Bakers. He asks Hamilton to prepare a suitable reply for his signature.

subfiles.title: The Bakers urge an end to war-material sales to Japan
subfiles.from: Madeleine H. Baker and Walter Baker
subfiles.about: Calls for a rapid halt to American shipments of weapons and other war materials after the writers viewed Walter Judd’s lecture and films.
subfiles.summary: The Bakers describe Judd’s images of Japanese brutality against Chinese civilians and argue that American supplies prolong the slaughter. They urge the government to stop exports of weapons, aircraft, tanks, scrap iron, and other military materials to Japan.

subfiles.title: Welles replies to Walter Baker
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the Bakers’ views and encloses the Department’s statement on shipments to China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Welles says the Department welcomes and carefully considers public opinions on foreign relations. He encloses the standard departmental statement concerning war-material shipments to China and Japan.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs legal assessment of Oregon picketing
subfiles.about: Concludes that the Department has no proper role in Oregon picketing unless international law or agreements are infringed.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum records Mr. Ward’s view that the reported incidents had already been satisfactorily resolved and disclosed no basis for departmental action. It recommends that Ballantine communicate this position informally to Kase if the issue arises again.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Kase about Oregon vessel picketing
subfiles.about: Records the Japanese Embassy’s presentation of information about Chinese picketing of Japanese ships loading scrap iron in Oregon.
subfiles.summary: Kase gives Ballantine an informal memorandum on incidents at Astoria and Portland. He suggests that State Department contact with Oregon’s governor might strengthen local efforts to resolve the dispute, while Ballantine notes that some difficulties appear settled. The Embassy primarily seeks to inform the Department and obtain any suggestions it may offer.

subfiles.title: Chronology of picketing at Oregon ports
subfiles.about: Chronicles Chinese picketing and longshoremen’s work stoppages affecting ships loading scrap iron at Astoria, Coos Bay, and Portland.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum describes picketing of the Norway Maru, a Mitsui-chartered vessel at Coos Bay, and planned picketing of the Ukin Maru and Hakuba Maru. It records approaches by the Japanese consul to municipal and state authorities, contemplated port closures, and the resumption of loading at Astoria. It ends with a large Chinese demonstration and sympathetic longshoremen’s strike against the Greek ship Ann Strathats in Portland.

subfiles.title: Second conversation with Kase on Oregon picketing
subfiles.about: Records Kase’s submission of an updated chronology and Ballantine’s view that no departmental action was yet warranted.
subfiles.summary: Kase provides a new memorandum whose first two pages repeat the March 6 chronology and whose third page records later events. Ballantine says that available facts do not appear to call for State Department action, though he continues to follow developments. Kase expresses appreciation without pressing the matter further.

subfiles.title: Updated chronology of Oregon vessel obstruction
subfiles.about: Updates the record of Chinese demonstrations and longshoremen’s refusals to load Japanese-connected vessels through March 14.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum repeats the early incidents and adds claims that demonstrators obstructed delivery of food to the Norway Maru. It records an Astoria Port Commission resolution ending future scrap-iron storage, an arbitrator’s ruling against the longshoremen, and further difficulties involving the Kostis and Uyo Maru. Portland officials reportedly say the federal government should address the disruption of Japanese-American trade.

subfiles.title: Hamilton reports refusal to involve State in Portland dispute
subfiles.about: Records Hamilton’s explanation to McNary that State Department intervention in the Portland labor dispute would be counterproductive.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton tells McNary that Welles and the Division have concluded State should not inject itself into the Portland situation. Because the immediate question concerns whether federal law prohibits scrap-iron exports, Hamilton says any authoritative statement should come from the Department of Justice. McNary understands that State does not intend to act.

subfiles.title: Background and proposed response to McNary on Portland disturbances
subfiles.to: Sumner Welles and other Department officials
subfiles.about: Reviews Japanese, Oregon, and Labor Department approaches and recommends against State Department intervention.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum summarizes Kase’s March 6 approach and the legal opinion that no action was appropriate absent an infringement of international law. It reports that Portland might close its port and that longshoremen were disregarding an arbitration award. The recommended response is that McNary or the Department of Justice, rather than State, could address the absence of a federal prohibition on scrap-iron exports.

subfiles.title: McNary seeks assistance after Oregon governor’s telegram
subfiles.about: Records McNary’s request for possible federal assistance in ending Chinese demonstrations and longshoremen’s refusal to load scrap iron.
subfiles.summary: McNary reads Hamilton a telegram from Governor Charles A. Sprague warning that the Portland port might close and asking State to tell local authorities that interference could endanger relations with Japan. Hamilton asks whether local law had been violated, but McNary has no definite information. The Department promises to consider the matter and respond later that day.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Oregon-picketing memoranda to Tokyo
subfiles.about: Sends the embassy copies of memoranda concerning picketing of Japanese vessels at Oregon ports.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary forwards the March 6 and March 15 conversation records and associated departmental memoranda. The enclosure list is intended to keep the American ambassador informed of the Oregon dispute and the Department’s handling of it.

subfiles.title: Havenner forwards Chinese American Citizens Alliance protest
subfiles.about: Requests the Department’s position on an appeal to stop credits and war-material shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Havenner reproduces a letter from the Chinese American Citizens Alliance describing civilian bombing, devastation, displacement, and casualties in China. The Alliance argues that American relief for China is contradicted by the sale of scrap iron and military materials to Japan. It urges Congress and the government to end the trade, and Havenner asks the Department to state its attitude.

subfiles.title: Hull explains policy to Havenner
subfiles.about: Describes the aeronautical-export policy, reports the cessation of arms-export licenses to Japan, and explains that scrap iron cannot be restricted under current law.
subfiles.summary: Hull sends the Department’s statement, the National Munitions Control Board report, and the January 12 press release. He says the entire American aircraft industry is now observing the Department’s policy against supplying countries that bomb civilians and that no arms-export licenses for Japan have been sought or issued in the previous two months. He nevertheless emphasizes that existing law provides no authority to prohibit or restrict scrap-iron exports.

subfiles.title: Welles asks Hamilton to answer World Peace Foundation letter
subfiles.about: Requests a draft reply to the latest World Peace Foundation communication.
subfiles.summary: Welles directs Hamilton to prepare an appropriate response for his signature. The note serves as an internal routing instruction for the Jones correspondence.

subfiles.title: Jones sends resolutions to Welles
subfiles.about: Sends the World Peace Foundation resolutions, highlighting the resolution against continued supply of Japan.
subfiles.summary: Jones calls Welles’s attention particularly to the resolution on war materials for Japan and suggests it may interest the Division of Far Eastern Affairs. He authorizes whatever use of the resolutions the Department considers advisable.

subfiles.title: World Peace Foundation resolutions
subfiles.from: Trustees of the World Peace Foundation
subfiles.to: U.S. Department of State and the public
subfiles.about: Calls for ending war-material supplies to Japan, maintaining American preparedness, and granting the President flexible neutrality powers.
subfiles.summary: The trustees condemn continued supply of Japan’s war in China and accept that ending it may require American economic sacrifices. They support naval and military preparedness and reaffirm their 1935 endorsement of broad presidential discretion over embargoes and trade restrictions. They reject rigid advance rules as ineffective and dangerous.

subfiles.title: Welles acknowledges Jones’s resolutions
subfiles.about: Thanks Jones for the resolutions and reiterates that their subjects are receiving careful consideration.
subfiles.summary: Welles acknowledges the March 20 letter and the enclosed February 11 resolutions. He notes them with interest and refers to the Department’s March 6 assurance that the issues are under careful review.

subfiles.title: Church requests seventy-five more statements
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the previous shipment and asks for seventy-five additional copies of the China-Japan war-material statement.
subfiles.summary: Church thanks the Acting Secretary for the March 23 letter and fifty copies already supplied. He requests seventy-five more for further distribution.

subfiles.title: Hull sends Church seventy-five statements
subfiles.about: Transmits the requested seventy-five additional copies of the Department’s statement.
subfiles.summary: Hull acknowledges Church’s March 28 request. The Department sends seventy-five copies of its statement on war-material exports to China and Japan.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to proposed Manchukuo steel purchase
subfiles.about: Points to a memorandum concerning a proposed $11 million American steel purchase for construction in Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: The note cross-references file 895.60 Manchuria/15. It describes Hornbeck’s conversation with Thomas W. Lamont about a Japanese proposal to buy steel from U.S. Steel through the Guaranty Trust Company for use in Manchukuo.

subfiles.title: Lewis thanks Yost for export information
subfiles.about: Thanks Yost for his April 4 response concerning exports of war supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Lewis briefly acknowledges receipt of Yost’s letter. He expresses appreciation for the information about war-supply exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: Lewis asks Hull about American support for Japan
subfiles.about: Asks whether the United States supplies more than half of Japan’s imported war needs and whether that aid can be reduced.
subfiles.summary: Lewis cites a circular from the American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression, identifying Henry L. Stimson and several honorary vice-chairmen. He asks Hull to verify its claim about American supplies and to consider action consistent with the Good Neighbor policy. He presents himself as an interested citizen who trusts Hull’s judgment.

subfiles.title: Yost replies to Lewis with export statement and arms definition
subfiles.about: Provides the Department’s statement and a pamphlet defining arms, ammunition, and implements of war.
subfiles.summary: Yost acknowledges Lewis’s March 29 inquiry about exports to Japan. He encloses the departmental statement and the pamphlet International Traffic in Arms, which reproduces the President’s May 1, 1937 proclamation defining controlled war matériel.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference for file 894.24/631
subfiles.about: Directs users from file 894.24/631 to file 811.34/1002.
subfiles.summary: This is a minimal cross-reference slip. It contains only the originating and destination file numbers and no substantive text.

subfiles.title: Harter forwards Foster’s petition and asks about current exports
subfiles.about: Requests comment on an Ohio petition and asks whether aircraft and munitions exports have stopped while oil, gasoline, scrap iron, and other materials remain freely available to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Harter encloses a letter apparently from Will J. Foster and an accompanying resolution. Before replying, he asks Hull to confirm his understanding of the distinction between direct military exports and unrestricted commodities usable for war.

subfiles.title: Foster sends anti-aggression petitions
subfiles.about: Transmits signed petitions from Elyria residents opposing American commerce that aids Japan’s war against China.
subfiles.summary: Foster reports universal opposition in his community to commercial assistance for Japan. He says no one asked to sign has refused and that most signatures were collected at meetings of his church.

subfiles.title: Elyria petition for non-participation in aggression
subfiles.from: 106 residents in and around Elyria, Ohio
subfiles.about: Demands a policy stopping shipment to aggressor nations of goods usable by their armed forces and calls for peaceful aid to China.
subfiles.summary: The petition condemns the use of American aircraft, gasoline, and munitions in bombing Chinese cities and calls profits from those sales hypocritical and bloodstained. It urges a Policy of Non-Participation in Aggression, an immediate halt to relevant shipments to Japan, and all peaceful measures possible to assist China. The copy notes that the original carried 106 signatures.

subfiles.title: Hull replies to Harter on exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Explains the policy discouraging aeronautical exports to countries bombing civilians and reports that no arms-export licenses to Japan had recently been requested or issued.
subfiles.summary: Hull sends copies of the Department’s statement for Harter and possible transmission to Foster, along with the National Munitions Control Board report and January 12 press release. He says all American aeronautical manufacturers and exporters are complying with the Department’s announced policy. No licenses for arms, ammunition, or implements of war to Japan had been applied for or issued during the preceding two months, and Foster’s letter and petition are returned.

subfiles.title: Beatrice Wright advocates an embargo on war materials
subfiles.about: Argues that Japan’s dependence on American machinery and lubricating oil gives the United States powerful leverage for an embargo.
subfiles.summary: Wright cites Eliot Janeway’s account of Japanese dependence on American machine tools and specialized lubricants and argues that withholding replacements could cripple armament production. She links American trade with Japan to broader fascist expansion involving Germany, Italy, and Nationalist Spain, and warns of danger to the Dutch East Indies and democracy generally. She urges an embargo before the strategic balance shifts further.

subfiles.title: Welles acknowledges Wright’s embargo appeal
subfiles.about: Thanks Wright for her views and sends the Department’s statement on exports to Japan and China.
subfiles.summary: Welles assures Wright that her observations on the Far Eastern situation will receive careful consideration. He encloses the Department’s standard statement concerning current war-material exports to Japan and China.
